newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: EU, NATO entry top C.Europe leaders talks.
newsitem.headline: EU, NATO entry top C.Europe leaders talks.

text.p: Presidents of eight central European states met in the Slovenian resort of Piran on Friday for talks focused on the chances of ex-communist states joining Europe's top political and military clubs.

The presidents of Germany, Italy and Austria, all members of the European Union, were joined by heads of state from the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia, former communist states which have made joining the European Union and NATO their main foreign policy goals.

The two-day meeting in the picturesque Adriatic town had as its advertised theme "the nation state in an integrated Europe" but it became clear that swift entry into the 15-nation EU and the NATO military alliance topped the agenda in bilateral talks and a plenary session.

Slovenian President Milan Kucan, hosting the fourth annual meeting of the heads of state, cautioned Western leaders that they should not exclude nations that met the conditions for membership of the two organisations.
"This is a time of cooperation and integration not a time of exclusion and division," Kucan, president of the former Yugoslav state for the past six years, said in a speech opening the meeting.
"Formal inclusion in the EU and NATO would be proof that the time of division (in Europe) is over for good and that our return finally has taken place."

The meeting, the first significant gathering of foreign leaders in Slovenia since independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, is taking place 10 days ahead of an EU summit at which leaders are expected to sign a treaty designed to prepare the EU for enlargement into eastern Europe.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland seem safe bets to be among the first nations to be invited to hold negotiations with Brussels over future membership.
Slovenia, which fought a 10-day war against Belgrade to gain its independence, has lobbied hard to be included in both the EU and NATO and has been backed by neighbouring Italy.

Slovakia, once a near-certainty, was sure to be left out of the first round after international criticism of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's government for failing to push through enough democratic reforms.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland were also certain to be invited to join NATO at a summit of alliance leaders in Madrid in July.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said after brief talks with Kucan that Warsaw had received guarantees that it would be invited to join NATO at Madrid.
He also said Poland was ready to support Slovenia in its bid to be in the first wave of enlargement, the Slovenian press agency STA reported.

After the first day of talks, the presidents attended a concert by Slovenian opera singer Marjana Lipovsek in a Piran monastery. A joint news conference at 0800 GMT on Saturday will be followed by a cruise along the Slovenian coast.
